statement: The services that customers and other outside parties depend on are listed, and written criteria decide which are critical. Resilience objectives are set for each critical service, and the critical services and their objectives are shared with the parties that rely on or deliver them, for example through service agreements or a distributed continuity plan. The list is reviewed on a defined cycle. This keeps recovery effort aimed at what outsiders cannot do without.
why_asked: If the organization has never said which services are critical, recovery priorities are guesses and customers promised one thing get another. Consultants look for written criteria and proof that the commitments reached outside parties.
how_to_ask: Ask for the list of services customers depend on and how criticality was decided. Then ask where customers and key suppliers are told what is promised. Example probe: "Which three services could you least afford to lose, who decided that and by what rule, and where do your customers see the objective?"
question: Does your organization decide which services outside parties depend on are critical, using written criteria?
expected_evidence: Register of services external parties depend on with criticality marked; written criticality criteria or impact analysis method; resilience objectives for each critical service; service agreements, customer agreements or continuity plan distribution records showing communication to relying and delivering parties; covering the current version and last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: A register lists the services outsiders rely on, marks which are critical and cites the written criteria used. Resilience objectives are set for each critical service. Agreements or distribution records show the objectives reached the parties that rely on or deliver those services.
test: Obtain the register and the criteria and confirm services are marked critical by those criteria, with objectives set for each. Sample customer or supplier agreements or distribution records and confirm the critical services or objectives were communicated. Pass if the register, criteria and objectives exist and communication is evidenced.
baseline_risk: Critical services are not defined, so recovery priorities are arbitrary and outside parties get no clear commitments.

statement: An inventory records the external resources and services the organization's critical functions depend on, such as cloud hosting, facilities and key software providers, and the functions each supports. The dependencies are ranked by importance to critical services, and those that are single points of failure are identified. The inventory is shared with the people responsible for continuity and risk, for example through the continuity plan and risk register. This shows where one outside failure could stop the business.
why_asked: Hidden dependencies and single points of failure turn a supplier outage into a business outage. Consultants check that dependencies are ranked and that the dependency map has actually been shared for continuity and risk planning.
how_to_ask: Ask for the list of outside services each critical function needs and which of them have no alternative. Then ask where it is referenced in continuity and risk records. Example probe: "If your main hosting provider failed tomorrow, which functions stop, and where is that written down?"
question: Does your organization keep a ranked map of the external services its critical functions depend on?
expected_evidence: Inventory of external dependencies mapped to business functions; ranking of dependencies by importance to critical services; list of single points of failure; continuity plan or risk register entries referencing the dependencies; covering the current version and last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: An inventory ties each outside resource to the functions it supports and ranks them by importance. Single points of failure are named in writing. The continuity plan or risk register references the map, and a record shows the map was shared for continuity and risk planning.
test: Obtain the inventory and confirm it links external dependencies to critical functions, ranks them and names single points of failure. Check that the continuity plan or risk register references the dependency information. Pass if the inventory is complete, ranked, flags single points of failure and has been shared for continuity and risk planning.
baseline_risk: Single points of failure outside the organization go unseen until one fails and critical services stop.

statement: Backups and other restoration assets are checked for integrity and compromise before they are used, for example by a malware scan or checksum, and the checks are recorded. After restoration, restored systems are verified before return to production, and normal operation is confirmed and recorded for each system, in priority order. This prevents restoring corrupted or infected data into production. Proof is the recovery procedure, the integrity check records and the sign-offs.
why_asked: Restoring an infected or corrupted backup can bring the attack back or deliver unusable data. Consultants test that checks happen before and after restore, beyond proving that a restore technically works.
how_to_ask: Ask what is checked on a backup before it is restored and what is checked on the system afterward. Then ask for the records from a recent restore or incident. Example probe: "Before you restored last time, how did you know the backup was clean, and who signed that the system was ready?"
question: Does your organization verify the integrity of backups and restored systems before they return to production?
expected_evidence: Recovery procedure requiring integrity and compromise checks and confirmation of normal operation; restore test or recovery records showing scan or checksum results before restore; post-restore verification records; sign-offs on return to operations; restoration priority order; covering the last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: The procedure requires checking backups and other restoration assets for integrity and compromise before use, and checking restored assets and confirming normal status before production. Records show the checks were done, restoration followed the priority order and each system was signed off.
test: Read the recovery procedure and confirm it requires checks before restoring and verification after. Sample restore tests and recoveries from the review period and confirm each has recorded integrity check results, post-restore verification, and sign-off in the agreed priority order. Pass if the requirement exists and every sampled recovery shows all three.
baseline_risk: Compromised or corrupt backups are restored into production, reinfecting systems or returning bad data.
